title: How do you practise cases with a partner and give useful feedback?
description: How to run a practice case for a friend, what good feedback sounds like, and how to get the most out of practising together.
hook: Practising with another person is where case skills really come together. It adds the pressure of someone watching, and it gives you feedback you cannot get alone. But many practice sessions are less useful than they could be: the interviewer reads too much out at once, or the feedback is just "that was good". Here is how to make each session count, whichever side of the table you are on.
body:
When you are the interviewer

  • Read the prompt and stop. Let the candidate recap and ask questions. Only share information when they ask for it, or when the case calls for it.
  • Hold back the data. If they do not ask for something, do not offer it. That is part of what is being tested.
  • Stay neutral. Do not nod at right answers or frown at wrong ones. Real interviewers often give little away.
  • Keep time. Most cases should take 25 to 35 minutes.

Giving feedback that helps

  • Be specific. Not "your structure was okay" but "your structure missed the market side, so you didn't check whether competitors had the same problem."
  • Pick the one thing. Name the single change that would have made the biggest difference.
  • Say what worked. People repeat what they know was good.
  • Use the six areas: recap and questions, structure, maths and charts, driving the case, recommendation, communication.

When you are the candidate

  • Treat it like the real thing: dress the part if it helps, use paper, speak out loud.
  • Ask for honest feedback, and write down the one thing to fix.
  • Do not argue with feedback in the moment. Ask questions to understand it.

No business background? No problem

Your partner does not need to know business. Any case with an interviewer script can be run by a friend. Every case in the PrepForCase casebook has one.

An example of useful feedback

Strong: clear recap, and your maths was right first time. To improve: your structure had "market" and "competition" as separate buckets that overlapped, so you checked rivals twice. Next time, put competitors inside the market bucket. One thing to practise this week: three structures a day, checking each for overlap before you speak.

Notice the shape: one strength, one specific fix with the reason, one practice task.
